planting.note: Direct sow in spring or start indoors and transplant after frost; plants are slow to flower the first year and bloom more fully in their second season.

directions: This tall Mediterranean relative of common marshmallow produces deeply lobed, hemp-like leaves on wiry, branching stems topped from midsummer into fall with a long succession of small pale pink, five-petaled flowers. Unlike the stouter Althaea officinalis, it has an airy, see-through habit that works well toward the back of a cottage or wildflower border where its flowers can be appreciated against sturdier neighbors. Give it full sun and well-drained soil, since it is less tolerant of constant moisture than medicinal marshmallow and can flop or rot in heavy wet ground. Established plants self-sow modestly and generally do not need staking except in very exposed sites.

planting.note: Sow in fall or very early spring so seed experiences a period of cold; plants form a basal rosette the first year and flower, set seed, and die in the second year.

directions: Common teasel is the wild, softer-spined relative of cultivated fuller's teasel, forming a coarse rosette of prickly-veined leaves in its first year before sending up a tall, branched, spiny stem crowned with egg-shaped flower heads ringed by small lavender florets in its second summer. Goldfinches and other seed-eating birds favor the dried heads heavily through winter, making it a worthwhile addition to a wildlife or dried-arrangement planting, though spent heads should be cut and removed where self-sowing beyond a contained area is unwanted, since it naturalizes readily in many regions. Grow it in an out-of-the-way sunny spot with average, well-drained soil; it needs no feeding or staking and tolerates poor, disturbed ground better than richer garden soil. Treat it as a short-lived biennial, replacing spent plants with fresh rosettes from self-sown or hand-sown seed.
sources: USDA Forest Service Plant of the Week

planting.note: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost and transplant out after danger of frost, or direct sow in fall in mild climates.

directions: This white-flowered selection of cupid's dart carries the same papery, straw-textured bracts as the familiar blue species but opens to pure white blooms with a small darker eye, giving a crisper, more old-fashioned look in a dried-flower or cottage border. Flowers are produced over a long summer season on wiry stems above a tidy clump of grassy, silvery-grey foliage, and both fresh and dried flower heads hold their shape well for cutting. Grow it in lean, sharply drained soil in full sun, since rich, moist conditions encourage floppy growth and shorten the plant's naturally short lifespan as a perennial. It performs best where summers are warm and dry, and is often grown as a short-lived perennial or replaced every few years from fresh seed.

planting.note: Start seed indoors in mid-to-late summer for fall planting of blooming-size transplants, or sow in very early spring for spring bedding.

directions: Tasso Rose is part of a large-flowered, fully double English daisy series bred for uniform, early, and extended bedding display, producing dense, quilled rose-pink flower heads held just above a compact mound of spoon-shaped leaves. Its larger flower size and more vigorous habit compared to older daisy strains make it reliable for mass plantings, edging, and container combinations with pansies or violas through the cool season. Grow in fertile, moist, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade, keeping plants evenly watered since they decline quickly in hot, dry conditions. Shear or deadhead spent flowers to extend bloom, and treat as a cool-season annual or short-lived biennial, discarding plants once summer heat sets in.
